title: The preachers, women and men
hookLine: he sends out preachers to lead sangats, women among them, and speaks against the burning of widows
last: PANGAT — NOBODY SITS AT THE HEAD.

cards: When something starts to grow, a small business, a club, a movement, there comes a moment when the founder can't be everywhere. People are joining in towns far away.

They want to learn, and they can't all travel to one village by the river. That's where the Sikhs were by the time of Guru Amar Das, with communities across the Punjab and beyond. So the Guru did something practical.
He chose trusted people and sent them out, each to look after a region, teach the hymns and gather the community. And tradition says some of those he trusted with this were women.

teach.h: MANJI — A COT, THEN A TEACHING SEAT.
teach.b: The word is manji. A manji is a simple cot, a low wooden frame strung with rope, the kind people sat on in Punjabi courtyards. The teacher sat on the manji, and the community gathered on the ground around it.
So manji came to mean the teaching post itself: the seat, and the responsibility that went with it.
Sikh tradition speaks of twenty-two manjis set up by Guru Amar Das, spreading the teaching across a wide region. And tradition says women were among those trusted to teach and lead.

The Guru also spoke directly about women's lives. One practice of that time and place was sati, the burning of a widow on her husband's funeral fire. In a hymn in the scripture, Guru Amar Das redefines the word.

teach.h: A TRUE SATI LIVES, IN GOODNESS.
teach.b: A true sati, he says, is not a woman who burns herself on her husband's pyre; it's one who lives with goodness and contentment, and honors her beloved by how she lives.
He's also remembered for discouraging the veil for women at the gathering, and for standing against the idea that a woman's worth ended with her husband's life.
Behind it all is a line of Guru Nanak's that Sikhs quote often.
Why call her lesser, he asks, from whom kings are born?
We are born of woman, we are married to woman, it is through woman that the world goes on. To be honest, Sikh communities, like others, have lived up to this unevenly.
But the Gurus' words are clear, and they're in the book.

how: In Sikh practice any person, woman or man, may lead prayer, read from the Guru Granth Sahib or perform kirtan; Sikhs cite Guru Nanak's words on women and Guru Amar Das's teaching on sati as part of the Gurus' stand for women's equality.

games.q: you're Guru Amar Das. communities are springing up far from Goindval, and they need teachers. whom do you trust with a manji?
o: no one; everyone must come to you.
games.why: tradition says he sent out trusted teachers to lead the sangats, and some were women.

practice: Bring to mind one woman who taught you: a mother or grandmother, a teacher, a boss, an older sister, a neighbor, a friend, someone who sat, in a way, on a manji for you. Remember one thing she taught you, in words or without them.
If she's alive, think how you'd tell her; if she's gone, just thank her, quietly.

wordCard.voice: Manji. A simple rope cot, and the teaching seat Guru Amar Das gave trusted women and men to lead communities. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: manji, a low rope-strung cot; the teacher sat on it, and the name came to mean the teaching post.

carryVoice: Your line: she is not lesser. Tomorrow, the song of bliss. That's day fifty-two, well spent.
